raw_case_text: In May 2002, a 33-year-old Italian man presented to our outpatient clinic complaining of fever, weight loss, and diarrhea. He had mucocutaneous lesions highly suggestive of Kaposi's sarcoma (KS). On physical examination he had hepatosplenomegaly; laboratory tests showed pancytopenia and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. He tested HIV positive. His CD4+ T-cell count was 17 cells/muL and HIV RNA viral load was 225,181 copies/mL. A bone marrow smear showed the presence of Leishmania spp. amastigotes. As a consequence, diagnosis of VL was made and treatment with meglumine antimoniate at a dose of 20 mg/kg/day was given for 30 days. Moreover, HAART with Lamivudine-Stavudine-Lopinavir/ritonavir was started. The patient clinically improved, with progressive resolution of KS lesions and good virological response to antiretroviral therapy. Six months later, the patient suffered a clinical relapse of VL and was treated with intravenous liposomal Amphotericin B (L-AMB) at a dose of 4 mg/kg/day for 5 days and then weekly at the same dose for 4 weeks. However, several relapses of VL occurred over the following years. Each relapse was treated with the aforementioned drug schedule. In February 2008, it was decided to start maintenance therapy with L-AMB at a dose of 4 mg/kg/day once a month, in an attempt to prevent further relapses. At this time, his HAART regimen consisted of Abacavir-Lamivudine-Lopinavir/ritonavir; HIV viral load was stably below 50 copies/mL and CD4+ T-cell count was 125 cells/muL. Some weeks after starting secondary prophylaxis with L-AMB, a maculopapular and nodular rash appeared on his trunk and upper limbs (Figure 1). The rash gradually worsened and, four months later, treatment with L-AMB was stopped and a cutaneous biopsy was performed. Histology revealed the presence of a granulomatous infiltrate, with lymphocytes, plasma cells, and macrophages, most of which contained Leishmania amastigotes. Restriction fragment length polymorphism-polymerase chain reaction (RFLP-PCR) was positive for L. infantum. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of PKDL. In September 2008, the patient started complaining of fever, diarrhea, and night sweats. Paradoxically, cutaneous lesions markedly improved. On the basis of his symptoms, a relapse of VL was suspected and confirmed by bone marrow aspirate, which showed the presence of Leishmania amastigotes. Treatment with meglumine antimoniate was restarted at a dose of 20 mg/kg/day for 30 days. The patient experienced a rapid clinical response and complete disappearance of cutaneous rash. Unfortunately, the patient had several relapses of VL over the following years, though the interval between them has become wider after restarting maintenance therapy with L-AMB 4 mg/kg/day once a month. At the last followup in December 2013, the patient was in good health and was still receiving secondary prophylaxis with L-AMB. He was taking HAART with Abacavir-Lamivudine-Lopinavir/ritonavir-raltegravir with his last CD4+ T-cell count being 98 cells/muL and HIV RNA < 20 copies/mL.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 33-year-old male presented with fever, weight loss, diarrhea, and mucocutaneous lesions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In May 2002, a 33-year-old male presented to an outpatient clinic with fever, weight loss, diarrhea, and mucocutaneous lesions suggestive of Kaposi's sarcoma. He was diagnosed with HIV infection and a systemic parasitic disease and received targeted antimicrobial therapy and HAART. Six months later, he experienced a clinical relapse and was treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (L-AMB) at 4 mg/kg/day for 5 days, then weekly for 4 weeks. Several relapses occurred over subsequent years, each managed with the same regimen. In February 2008, secondary prophylaxis with monthly L-AMB (4 mg/kg/day) was started. Weeks later, he developed a maculopapular and nodular rash on the trunk and upper limbs, which gradually worsened over 4 months, leading to L-AMB discontinuation and skin biopsy. In September 2008, he developed fever, diarrhea, and night sweats while the rash improved. Relapse was diagnosed and treated with antimonials, resulting in rapid symptom resolution and rash clearance. Subsequent relapses occurred with longer inter-relapse intervals on monthly L-AMB. At follow-up in December 2013, he remained in good health on secondary prophylaxis.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection diagnosed in 2002; Kaposi's sarcoma. Prior antiretroviral therapy: initial HAART with lamivudine, stavudine, and lopinavir/ritonavir; switched in 2008 to abacavir, lamivudine, and lopinavir/ritonavir; later intensified with raltegravir. Prior antimicrobial therapy with antimonials and liposomal amphotericin B.
subjective.review_of_systems: Fever, weight loss, diarrhea, night sweats, maculopapular and nodular skin rash. Denied other acute complaints.

objective.physical_examination: Hepatosplenomegaly present on abdominal examination; mucocutaneous lesions suggestive of Kaposi's sarcoma. Subsequent examination revealed a maculopapular and nodular rash distributed across the trunk and upper limbs.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory testing revealed pancytopenia and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. Initial CD4+ T-cell count: 17 cells/muL; HIV RNA viral load: 225,181 copies/mL. In February 2008: CD4+ T-cell count: 125 cells/muL; HIV RNA viral load stably < 50 copies/mL. In December 2013: CD4+ T-cell count: 98 cells/muL; HIV RNA viral load < 20 copies/mL.
objective.advanced_workup: Cutaneous biopsy histology demonstrated a dermal granulomatous infiltrate composed of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and macrophages containing intracellular microorganisms. Serial bone marrow aspirates and smears demonstrated hypercellularity with macrophages containing intracellular protozoal forms.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Recurrent visceral leishmaniasis (VL) and post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) in a patient with advanced HIV-1 coinfection.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Initial bone marrow smear (May 2002) revealed Leishmania spp. amastigotes. Cutaneous biopsy histology showed macrophages containing Leishmania amastigotes, and RFLP-PCR was positive for Leishmania infantum, confirming PKDL. September 2008 relapse confirmed by repeat bone marrow aspirate demonstrating Leishmania amastigotes.
Differentials Ruled Out: Kaposi's sarcoma (mucocutaneous lesions initially suspected; resolved with HAART), other opportunistic infections, and drug eruptions.
Treatment & Clinical Course: Initial VL treated with meglumine antimoniate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) and HAART (lamivudine-stavudine-lopinavir/ritonavir) with clinical improvement. Relapses treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (L-AMB; 4 mg/kg/day for 5 days then weekly for 4 weeks). In February 2008, secondary prophylaxis with monthly L-AMB (4 mg/kg/day) was initiated. September 2008 relapse treated with meglumine antimoniate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) with complete rash clearance and symptom resolution. Monthly L-AMB maintenance was resumed, successfully widening relapse intervals. In December 2013, the patient was clinically well on L-AMB prophylaxis and abacavir-lamivudine-lopinavir/ritonavir-raltegravir.
